metadata.title: Undersea Arteries: How Subsea Fiber Optic Cables Power the Global Internet
metadata.subtitle: An Engineering Explainer on Deep-Ocean Telecom, Repeaters, and Fault Recovery
metadata.author: LexaWrites Press

cable_layers_from_center.Role: Carries laser light signals across 16 fiber pairs
Blocks hydrogen ingress and conducts 10,000V DC power
Provides mechanical tensile strength during ship laying
Insulates high-voltage copper from seawater ground

fault_causes_distribution.Mitigation: Double steel wire armoring and 2 m seabed burial
Designated cable protection corridors and AIS monitoring
Slack routing around canyons and rapid ship splicing
Redundant laser pumps and 25-year pressure housings

chapters.title: The Garden Hose on the Abyssal Plain
chapters.focus: Explain why 99% of intercontinental data travels through undersea fibers rather than satellites, and detail the 4 core physical layers that shrink a deep-sea cable down to 17 mm in diameter.

chapters.title: Fighting Photon Loss: Optical Attenuation and Erbium Repeaters
chapters.focus: Explain silica glass attenuation (0.15 dB/km) and how Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifiers (EDFAs) placed every 70 km boost light signals purely optically without slowing them down to electronics.

chapters.title: The 10,000-Volt Copper Spine and Seawater Grounding
chapters.focus: Explain how shore Power Feeding Equipment (PFE) pushes 10,000V DC at 1.1 Amps through the cable's copper tube to power repeaters across oceans, and how single-end power feeding survives a ground fault.

chapters.title: Wavelength Division Multiplexing and 384-Terabit Capacity
chapters.focus: Explain how 16 hair-thin fiber pairs carry 24 Tbps each (384 Tbps total) by splitting laser light into dozens of distinct color wavelengths within the 1550 nm C-band window.

chapters.title: Continental Shelves, Trawlers, and Trenching Plows
chapters.focus: Contrast the 17 mm deep-sea lightweight cable with the 50 mm double-armored shallow-water cable, explaining why fishing trawlers (40%) and ship anchors (30%) require burying cables 2 meters under the seabed.

chapters.title: Deep-Sea Surgery: Finding and Splicing a Severed Cable
chapters.focus: Detail how engineers pinpoint breaks within meters using Optical Time-Domain Reflectometry (OTDR), drag grapnels at 4,000 meters depth, and splice fibers aboard specialized repair ships.
